questions.question: Physically identifying an asset with its sensitivity or classification level (for example, a stamped "CONFIDENTIAL" label on a folder) is referred to as:

explanation.why_correct: Marking is the physical identification of an asset with its appropriate sensitivity or classification level.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Labeling is the digital/logical identification (e.g., metadata or watermarks).
why_others_are_wrong.D: Scoping selects which controls apply to a system.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Tailoring modifies baseline controls.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes physical marking from logical labeling.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Information and Asset Handling Requirements

questions.question: Embedding a classification level in a file's metadata or as a digital watermark is an example of:

explanation.why_correct: Labeling is the digital or logical identification of an asset with its sensitivity/classification, implemented through metadata or digital watermarks.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Marking is the physical identification of an asset.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Degaussing is a magnetic data-destruction method.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Tokenization substitutes sensitive data with non-sensitive tokens.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps metadata/watermark identification to logical labeling.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Information and Asset Handling Requirements

questions.question: An organization stamps "SECRET" on printed reports and embeds a "SECRET" tag in the metadata of the corresponding electronic files. The printed stamp and the metadata tag represent, respectively:

explanation.why_correct: The physical stamp is marking; the electronic metadata tag is labeling (logical identification).

why_others_are_wrong.A: This reverses the definitions—physical is marking, logical is labeling.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Scoping/tailoring are control-selection activities, not handling identification.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Clearing/purging are data-destruction techniques.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the physical-vs-logical distinction in a concrete handling example.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Information and Asset Handling Requirements

questions.question: Why should an organization define a consistent process for marking and labeling assets?

options.label: A
options.text: To make every asset Top Secret regardless of sensitivity

options.label: B
options.text: To ensure all personnel handle data correctly and support compliance, reducing breach and misuse risk

options.label: C
options.text: To guarantee assets never need to be inventoried

options.label: D
options.text: To avoid having to classify data at all

explanation.why_correct: A consistent marking/labeling process ensures correct, repeatable handling, supports compliance, and minimizes the risk of breaches or asset misuse.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Consistency is about correct handling, not over-classifying everything.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Consistent handling depends on classification, not its absence.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Inventory remains essential to asset management.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects consistent handling processes to compliance and risk reduction.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Organizational Policies

questions.question: When sensitive data is copied or backed up, those copies should be:

options.label: A
options.text: Treated as public since they are duplicates

options.label: B
options.text: Handled and stored according to the same sensitivity/classification as the original

options.label: C
options.text: Exempt from the data retention policy

options.label: D
options.text: Stored without any access controls to ease recovery

explanation.why_correct: Copies and backups must be handled and stored according to the data's sensitivity, just like the original.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Copies retain the original's sensitivity and are not public.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Backups of sensitive data still require access controls.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Retention policy applies to copies/backups as well.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces that backups inherit the original data's classification and handling.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Handling Sensitive Data and Assets

questions.question: In secure asset management, "provisioning" refers to:

options.label: D
options.text: Creating, managing, and destroying assets throughout their lifecycle

explanation.why_correct: Provisioning involves creating, managing, and destroying assets throughout their lifecycle.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Provisioning covers the full lifecycle, not only deletion of backups.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Marking is a handling activity, not provisioning.
why_others_are_wrong.A: SOX auditing is a compliance activity unrelated to provisioning definition.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of provisioning across the asset lifecycle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Managing System Assets

questions.question: An accurate asset inventory is described as crucial primarily because it:

options.label: A
options.text: Eliminates the need for any security controls

options.label: B
options.text: Enables effective change control and configuration management by accounting for all assets

options.label: C
options.text: Replaces the need for data classification

explanation.why_correct: An accurate inventory is crucial for implementing change control and configuration management and ensures all assets are accounted for throughout their lifecycle.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Inventory supports, but does not replace, security controls.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Inventory tracks assets; it does not perform patching itself.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Inventory and classification are complementary activities.

questions.exam_reasoning: Links inventory to change/configuration management.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Asset Management Components

questions.question: Who is described as accountable for overall asset management, including IT assets, hardware procurement, and asset disposal?

explanation.why_correct: Senior management is accountable for overall asset management, including IT assets, hardware, procurement, and disposal.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Data subjects are users/individuals interacting with data.
why_others_are_wrong.B: External auditors verify compliance; they are not accountable for asset management.
why_others_are_wrong.D: End users operate systems but are not accountable for overall asset management.

questions.exam_reasoning: Assigns overall asset-management accountability to senior management.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Responsibilities

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are HARDWARE assets that should be tracked in an inventory? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: Hardware to track includes servers, switches, firewalls, gateways, proxies, and IDS/IPS systems—both a firewall appliance and a network switch qualify.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A license key relates to software, not a hardware asset.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A policy is an administrative document, not a hardware asset.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes hardware assets from software and administrative items.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > What to Track

questions.question: Which approach uses tools such as Nmap or OpenVAS to discover hosts and identify operating systems for an asset inventory?

explanation.why_correct: Automated discovery uses tools like Nessus, Nmap, and OpenVAS for host discovery and OS identification.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Manual tracking uses spreadsheets/databases, not automated scanning tools.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Degaussing is a data-destruction method.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Tokenization is a data-protection/declassification technique.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps host-discovery tooling to automated asset discovery.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Tools and Techniques for Asset Tracking

questions.question: To protect the asset inventory itself, an organization should ensure that:

options.label: A
options.text: The inventory is publicly editable to encourage updates

options.label: B
options.text: The inventory is never updated once created

options.label: C
options.text: Access to view and modify the inventory is restricted to authorized personnel and changes follow change control

options.label: D
options.text: Anyone may delete entries to keep the list short

explanation.why_correct: Inventory security and integrity require restricting access/modifications to authorized personnel and managing updates through configuration management and change control.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Public editability destroys integrity and enables tampering.
why_others_are_wrong.B: The inventory must be updated as assets change, via change control.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Uncontrolled deletion undermines accuracy and integrity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests protecting the integrity of the asset inventory.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Organizational Policy and Management

questions.question: The asset lifecycle (per NIST SP 1800-5) includes strategy, planning, design, procurement, operation, maintenance, modification, and:

explanation.why_correct: The asset lifecycle culminates in disposal, completing the cradle-to-grave management of assets.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Marketing is not part of the asset lifecycle.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Tokenization is a data-protection technique, not an asset-lifecycle phase.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Phishing is an attack technique, not a lifecycle phase.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of disposal as the final asset-lifecycle phase.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Key Concepts

questions.question: Regulations such as GDPR and HIPAA most directly influence which aspect of asset security?

options.label: A
options.text: The brand of laptop employees may purchase

options.label: D
options.text: How data is stored, accessed, transmitted, and destroyed (data handling)

explanation.why_correct: Regulations like GDPR and HIPAA shape data-handling practices—storage, access control, transmission, and destruction.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Laptop brand selection is procurement, not regulatory data handling.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Floor plans are facilities matters, not data-handling regulation.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Label color is a cosmetic detail, not the substance of handling rules.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects regulations to data-handling requirements.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Information and Asset Handling Requirements

questions.question: Which of the following operational details is appropriate to record for a tracked asset?

options.label: A
options.text: The personal hobbies of the employee who uses it

options.label: C
options.text: Purchase/installation date, licensing, location, and baseline configuration

explanation.why_correct: Operational details to track include purchase/installation dates, licensing, dependencies, location, IP addresses, and baseline configurations.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Personal hobbies are irrelevant to asset tracking.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Assets do not have a "favorite color"; this is not a tracked detail.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Marketing slogans are unrelated to asset records.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies legitimate operational tracking details.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > What to Track

questions.question: The guide describes data as existing in three states. Which set correctly lists them?

options.label: B
options.text: In use, in transit, and at rest

explanation.why_correct: Data exists in three states—in use, in transit, and at rest—each requiring appropriate protection.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Hot/warm/cold describe site recovery strategies, not data states.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Public/internal/secret are classification levels, not data states.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Create/read/delete are operations, not data states.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the three data states.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Understanding Data States

questions.question: Which protection mechanisms are MOST associated with securing data at rest?

options.label: A
options.text: Full-disk encryption, Trusted Platform Modules (TPM), and secure storage

options.label: C
options.text: Network egress monitoring on the perimeter

explanation.why_correct: Data at rest is protected with full-disk encryption, TPMs, and secure storage environments because it is a static target.

why_others_are_wrong.D: TLS and secure routing protect data in transit.
why_others_are_wrong.B: In-memory protections apply to data in use.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Egress monitoring targets data leaving the network (in transit/exfiltration), not data at rest.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps at-rest protections to encryption/TPM/secure storage.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Data at Rest

questions.question: Data is considered MOST at risk in which state, because it is exposed to the network?

explanation.why_correct: Data in transit is most at risk because it is exposed to the network (wired or wireless); it is protected with encryption, secure routing, and certificates (SSL/TLS).

why_others_are_wrong.A: Data at rest is a static target but is not described as the most-at-risk state.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Data in use is the most volatile but is being processed locally, not exposed across the network.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Archived data is a form of data at rest.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies in-transit as the most network-exposed state.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Understanding Data States

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes data in use?

options.label: A
options.text: It is always encrypted and never at risk

options.label: B
options.text: It only exists on backup tapes

options.label: C
options.text: It is data that has been permanently destroyed

options.label: D
options.text: It is the most volatile state, residing in memory or being processed, and needs authentication, authorization, and monitoring

explanation.why_correct: Data in use is actively processed (often in memory), is the most volatile state, and requires authentication, authorization, and monitoring to protect integrity.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Data in use can be at risk during processing and is not inherently always encrypted.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Backup tapes hold data at rest, not data in use.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Destroyed data is not a live state.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the volatility and controls for data in use.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Understanding Data States

questions.question: A company sends application logs from a web server to a remote analysis platform over the internet. Which protection is MOST appropriate for this data while it travels?

options.label: A
options.text: Full-disk encryption on the destination server only

options.label: B
options.text: A Trusted Platform Module on the source server

options.label: D
options.text: Encryption with mutual authentication (e.g., TLS) to protect data in motion

explanation.why_correct: Data in transit is best protected with encryption and mutual authentication (e.g., TLS) to defend confidentiality and integrity while it moves.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Disk encryption at the destination protects data at rest, not while it traverses the network.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A TPM protects keys/data at rest on a device, not data crossing the network.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Degaussing destroys data on magnetic media; it does not protect data in transit.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests selecting in-transit protection for a network transfer scenario.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Security Considerations

questions.question: Place the data lifecycle phases in their typical order from cradle to grave. (Provide the option labels in order.)

explanation.why_correct: The data lifecycle runs creation → storage → use → archiving → destruction (cradle to grave).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the order of the data lifecycle phases.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Managing the Data Lifecycle

questions.question: Immediately after data is created, what should occur to ensure it receives the right level of protection?

options.label: A
options.text: It should be made public by default

options.label: B
options.text: It should be classified or categorized according to its sensitivity

options.label: C
options.text: It should be moved straight to archive storage

explanation.why_correct: After creation, data must be classified/categorized by sensitivity so that appropriate protection is applied throughout its life.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Destruction is the final phase, not the step right after creation.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Defaulting to public would expose sensitive data.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Archiving applies to data no longer needed regularly, not freshly created data.

questions.exam_reasoning: Ties classification to the create phase of the lifecycle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Managing the Data Lifecycle

questions.question: When data that is no longer needed regularly is moved to archive storage, the guide states that archives must still have:

options.label: D
options.text: All security controls removed to save space

explanation.why_correct: Archived data must have access controls and encryption applied; archiving can be driven by regulatory or organizational requirements.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Removing controls would expose archived sensitive data.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Public access to archives risks unauthorized disclosure.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Retention limits and policies still apply to archived data.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces that archives remain protected.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Managing the Data Lifecycle

questions.question: A dataset that was highly sensitive at launch becomes far less sensitive years later as the information becomes obsolete. According to the guide's "data value over time" consideration, the organization should:

options.label: B
options.text: Immediately make the data public without review

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the original classification permanently regardless of changes

options.label: D
options.text: Re-evaluate the data's classification and adjust protection needs as its value changes

explanation.why_correct: Data value can change over time, affecting classification and protection needs; classification should be re-evaluated accordingly.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Static classification ignores legitimate changes in data value.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Reclassification requires review, not automatic public release.
why_others_are_wrong.A: The policy remains necessary to govern reclassification decisions.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests reclassification as data value changes over time.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Key Considerations

questions.question: In the destruction phase of the data lifecycle, secure destruction methods are required primarily to:

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the amount of stored data

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid the need to follow any regulations

options.label: C
options.text: Ensure no sensitive data can be recovered by unauthorized parties

explanation.why_correct: Secure destruction follows policy and legal/regulatory requirements and ensures that no sensitive data can be recovered by unauthorized parties.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Destruction removes data; it does not increase storage.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Destruction prevents access, not public searchability.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Destruction must comply with—not bypass—regulations.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects secure destruction to preventing recovery of sensitive data.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Managing the Data Lifecycle

questions.question: During the initiation phase of the information system lifecycle, the PRIMARY focus is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Identify and engage stakeholders and understand requirements and the system's purpose

options.label: B
options.text: Run the system in full production

options.label: C
options.text: Conduct the final retirement of the system

options.label: D
options.text: Securely erase all data and dispose of hardware

explanation.why_correct: Initiation focuses on identifying/engaging stakeholders (users, managers, customers, auditors, leadership) and understanding requirements and the system's purpose.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Erasure/disposal occurs at the disposal/retirement phase.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Full production occurs in operations and maintenance.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Retirement is the final phase, not initiation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps stakeholder/requirement understanding to the initiation phase.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > The Information System Lifecycle - Part 1

questions.question: The "development and acquisition" phase centers on which key decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Which classification color to use on labels

options.label: B
options.text: Whether to build the system in-house or buy/acquire a third-party solution, based on capability and security needs

options.label: C
options.text: How many press releases to issue

explanation.why_correct: Development and acquisition addresses the build-vs-buy decision, applying secure development practices internally or vetting third-party solutions for security.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Degaussing is a destruction method, not a build/buy decision.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Label color is a handling cosmetic, not a lifecycle decision.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Press releases are unrelated to the system lifecycle.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the build-vs-buy focus of the development/acquisition phase.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > The Information System Lifecycle - Part 1

questions.question: The disposal (retirement) phase of the information system lifecycle requires that:

options.label: C
options.text: All data is securely erased and hardware is disposed of so data cannot be recovered

options.label: D
options.text: The system is moved into full production use

explanation.why_correct: Disposal involves secure decommissioning—ensuring all data is securely erased and hardware is disposed of to prevent data recovery.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Production use is operations/maintenance, not disposal.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Requirement gathering is part of initiation.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Build-vs-buy is the development/acquisition phase.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps secure data erasure/hardware disposal to the disposal phase.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Disposal

questions.question: Which (now retired but still referenced) NIST publication provides a structured approach to embedding security into the information system lifecycle?

explanation.why_correct: NIST SP 800-64 Rev. 2, though retired, is still referenced for embedding security into the system development lifecycle.

why_others_are_wrong.B: NIST SP 800-60 covers data types and classification.
why_others_are_wrong.D: NIST SP 800-88 covers media sanitization.
why_others_are_wrong.C: NIST SP 800-137 covers information security continuous monitoring.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes lifecycle-security guidance (800-64) from related publications.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > Disposal

questions.question: A core principle emphasized across the information system lifecycle is that security should be:

options.label: A
options.text: Added only after a breach occurs

options.label: B
options.text: Left entirely to the end users

options.label: C
options.text: Integrated from the initial phases through disposal, at every step

options.label: D
options.text: Considered only during the disposal phase

explanation.why_correct: Security must be integrated from the initial phases through disposal—built in at every step rather than bolted on.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Waiting for a breach is reactive and leaves the system exposed.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Security must apply throughout, not only at disposal.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Security is a shared responsibility led by management, not solely end users.

questions.exam_reasoning: Reinforces security integration throughout the lifecycle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Asset Security > The Information System Lifecycle - Part 2

questions.question: A sound data retention policy holds that data should be retained:

options.label: A
options.text: Forever, regardless of need or regulation

options.label: B
options.text: For exactly 24 hours in all cases

options.label: C
options.text: Only if it is public data

options.label: D
options.text: Only as long as necessary or legally required, then securely destroyed

explanation.why_correct: Data should be retained securely and only for as long as necessary per organizational policy and legal/regulatory requirements, then destroyed.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Indefinite retention increases liability and breach exposure.
why_others_are_wrong.B: There is no universal 24-hour rule; retention depends on policy/regulation.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Retention applies to many data types, not only public data.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the retain-only-as-long-as-needed principle.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Data Retention Requirements

questions.question: A vendor announces it will no longer release patches or provide support for a server operating system, although the OS still technically runs. This status is called:

explanation.why_correct: End-of-Support (EOS) is when the vendor no longer maintains or supports the hardware/software, even if it still runs.

why_others_are_wrong.C: End-of-Life (EOL) is when the asset can no longer be used or the license expires.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Data remanence is leftover data after deletion attempts.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Tailoring out is removing controls from a baseline.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes EOS (no support) from EOL (no longer usable).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Retention Best Practices

questions.question: A critical application server has reached end-of-support, so it no longer receives security patches. From an asset-retention standpoint, the BEST action is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Remove all monitoring to reduce noise

options.label: B
options.text: Expose it directly to the internet to extend its usefulness

options.label: C
options.text: Keep running it indefinitely since it still functions

options.label: D
options.text: Replace or remove the unsupported asset to avoid security vulnerabilities

explanation.why_correct: When assets are no longer supported, they should be replaced or removed because unpatched systems introduce security vulnerabilities.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Running unsupported systems indefinitely leaves unpatched vulnerabilities exposed.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Internet exposure of an unpatched server dramatically increases risk.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Removing monitoring reduces visibility into an already-risky asset.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests responding to end-of-support assets.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Asset Retention

questions.question: Which TWO regulations/standards are cited as governing data retention requirements? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: HIPAA (healthcare) and PCI DSS (payment data) are among the regulations/standards governing data retention.

why_others_are_wrong.B: The Wassenaar Arrangement governs export controls, not data retention.
why_others_are_wrong.C: STRIDE is a threat-modeling methodology, not a retention regulation.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies retention-governing regulations among distractors.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Regulations Governing Data Retention

questions.question: Which standard focuses specifically on records management, including the concepts and principles of data retention?

explanation.why_correct: ISO 15489 focuses on records management, including data-retention concepts and principles.

why_others_are_wrong.C: ISO 27040 addresses storage security.
why_others_are_wrong.B: NIST SP 800-88 covers media sanitization.
why_others_are_wrong.D: PCI DSS is a payment-card security standard.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps records-management retention guidance to ISO 15489.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Guidance on Data Retention

questions.question: When data is involved in a legal or security investigation, what must be maintained to ensure its integrity is defensible?

explanation.why_correct: Chain of custody is a documented process tracking who accessed data, ensuring its integrity in legal proceedings; such data must be retained until the case concludes.

why_others_are_wrong.D: A marketing plan is irrelevant to evidentiary integrity.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A public changelog does not establish evidentiary control.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A EULA is a licensing agreement, not an evidence-integrity process.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects evidentiary integrity to chain of custody.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Retention and Legal Proceedings

questions.question: An organization's policy says to destroy a category of records after 18 months, but those exact records are now the subject of active litigation. The organization should:

options.label: A
options.text: Make the records public to resolve the dispute faster

options.label: B
options.text: Destroy them on schedule because policy takes precedence over litigation

options.label: C
options.text: Retain the records until the legal matter concludes, overriding the routine destruction schedule

options.label: D
options.text: Move the records off-site and stop tracking who accesses them

explanation.why_correct: Data involved in legal proceedings must be retained until the case concludes, and chain of custody maintained—this overrides routine destruction.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Destroying records under litigation can constitute spoliation and legal liability.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Public disclosure could violate confidentiality and harm the case.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Ceasing access tracking breaks chain of custody and undermines integrity.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests legal hold overriding scheduled destruction.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Retention and Legal Proceedings

questions.question: Which TWO elements should a well-formed data retention policy define? (Select TWO.)

options.label: A
options.text: End-of-life and end-of-support requirements for assets

options.label: B
options.text: The personal opinions of individual employees

options.label: C
options.text: Retention periods or timelines for the data

options.label: D
options.text: A list of competitor product prices

explanation.why_correct: A retention policy should define retention periods/timelines and EOL/EOS requirements (along with purpose/scope and data covered), aligned with legal/regulatory needs.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Personal opinions are not policy elements.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Competitor pricing is irrelevant to a retention policy.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies required contents of a retention policy.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Organizational Data Retention Policy

questions.question: In control selection, a "baseline" is BEST described as:

options.label: A
options.text: A control that is never modified

options.label: B
options.text: The maximum number of controls a system can hold

options.label: C
options.text: The minimum set of controls that serves as a starting point for protection

options.label: D
options.text: A method for destroying magnetic media

explanation.why_correct: A baseline is the minimum set of controls for safeguarding security/privacy (often from NIST SP 800-53 or ISO/IEC 27002) and acts as an adaptable starting point.

why_others_are_wrong.B: A baseline is a minimum starting point, not a maximum.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Baselines are adaptable through scoping and tailoring.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Destroying magnetic media is degaussing, unrelated to a control baseline.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the baseline as a minimum control starting point.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Baseline and Tailoring

questions.question: Selecting which controls from a baseline actually apply to a specific system or environment is called:

explanation.why_correct: Scoping determines which baseline controls are applicable to an organization's system or environment.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Tailoring in is adding controls beyond the baseline for new risks.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Degaussing is a data-destruction method.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Provisioning is creating/managing/destroying assets over their lifecycle.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes scoping (applicability) from tailoring.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Baseline and Tailoring

questions.question: Modifying a baseline by ADDING controls to address new risks or heightened data sensitivity is referred to as:

explanation.why_correct: Tailoring in is adding additional controls based on new risks or data sensitivity; tailoring out is removing controls that are not relevant.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Tailoring out removes controls that do not apply.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Scoping selects which baseline controls apply at all.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Sanitization is a data-destruction concept.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes tailoring in (add) from tailoring out (remove).

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Baseline and Tailoring

questions.question: A baseline includes a control requiring secure handling of wireless transmissions, but the target system is fully air-gapped with no wireless capability. The MOST appropriate action is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Leave the control and force the system to add wireless hardware

options.label: B
options.text: Tailor in additional wireless controls to be safe

options.label: C
options.text: Apply the high-watermark principle to add more controls

options.label: D
options.text: Tailor out the wireless control because it does not apply to this system

explanation.why_correct: Tailoring out removes baseline controls that are not relevant or applicable—an air-gapped system with no wireless does not need the wireless control.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Adding wireless controls to a system with no wireless wastes effort and is irrelevant.
why_others_are_wrong.C: High watermark addresses co-mingled sensitivity, not inapplicable controls.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Forcing wireless hardware to justify a control is backwards and increases risk.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests tailoring out an inapplicable control.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Baseline and Tailoring

questions.question: According to the control selection process, controls should be selected based primarily on:

options.label: A
options.text: Whichever controls are cheapest, regardless of risk

options.label: B
options.text: The personal preference of the newest administrator

options.label: C
options.text: The alphabetical order of control names

options.label: D
options.text: The level of risk and the protection needs of the information

explanation.why_correct: Controls are selected based on the level of risk and protection needs; over-securing public systems is avoided while sensitive systems receive appropriate controls.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Personal preference is not a valid selection basis.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Cost alone, ignoring risk, leads to under- or over-protection.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Alphabetical order is irrelevant to control selection.

questions.exam_reasoning: Ties control selection to risk and protection needs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Selection Process

questions.question: A public-facing website serves only non-sensitive marketing content. Applying the control selection principles, the team should:

options.label: A
options.text: Apply controls proportionate to the low sensitivity and avoid over-securing the public system

options.label: B
options.text: Classify the marketing content as Top Secret to be safe

options.label: C
options.text: Remove all controls because the data is public

options.label: D
options.text: Apply the same controls used for the most sensitive internal database

explanation.why_correct: Control selection avoids over-securing public systems; controls should be proportionate to the data's low sensitivity and risk.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Applying maximum internal controls to a public site wastes resources.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Even public systems need baseline protections (e.g., integrity, availability).
why_others_are_wrong.B: Over-classifying non-sensitive content misallocates protection effort.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests proportionate control selection to avoid over-securing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Selection Process

questions.question: Which framework, managed by ISACA, is designed for IT governance and aligning IT with business objectives?

explanation.why_correct: COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies), managed by ISACA, focuses on IT governance and aligning IT with business needs.

why_others_are_wrong.D: NIST SP 800-88 covers media sanitization.
why_others_are_wrong.A: ISO 15489 covers records management.
why_others_are_wrong.B: The Deming Cycle (PDCA) is a continuous-improvement model, not a governance framework.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps IT-governance framework to COBIT/ISACA.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Security Control Frameworks

questions.question: COBIT is derived from which framework, which is used to comply with Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) 404 and focuses on preventing fraudulent financial reporting?

explanation.why_correct: COBIT is derived from COSO; COSO is used for SOX 404 compliance and focuses on preventing fraudulent financial reporting.

why_others_are_wrong.A: ISO/IEC 27002 is an international code of practice for security controls.
why_others_are_wrong.D: HITRUST is a common security framework for health information.
why_others_are_wrong.B: NIST SP 800-53 is the U.S. federal control catalog required by FISMA.

questions.exam_reasoning: Connects COSO to SOX 404 and its relationship to COBIT.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Security Control Frameworks

questions.question: Which control framework is widely used by U.S. government organizations, is required by FISMA, and is organized into control families?

explanation.why_correct: NIST SP 800-53 provides security and privacy controls, is required by FISMA, and is organized into control families (e.g., access control, audit and accountability).

why_others_are_wrong.B: ISO 15489 is a records-management standard.
why_others_are_wrong.C: COBIT is an IT-governance framework, not the FISMA control catalog.
why_others_are_wrong.A: AACS is a DRM scheme for optical media.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps FISMA-required control families to NIST SP 800-53.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Common Security Control Standards

questions.question: Which international standard, originating from British Standard 7799, provides a widely adopted code of practice broken into control objectives (policies, HR security, cryptography, etc.)?

explanation.why_correct: ISO/IEC 27002 originated from BS 7799 (via 17799) and is an international standard of control objectives, widely adopted across industries.

why_others_are_wrong.B: NIST SP 800-37 is the Risk Management Framework process.
why_others_are_wrong.C: COSO is a financial-reporting/governance framework used for SOX.
why_others_are_wrong.A: PCI DSS is a payment-card security standard.

questions.exam_reasoning: Identifies ISO/IEC 27002 by its BS 7799 lineage and control-objective structure.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Security Control Frameworks

questions.question: Which common security framework is specifically associated with protecting health information?

explanation.why_correct: HITRUST (Health Information Trust Alliance) is a common security framework for health information.

why_others_are_wrong.A: COBIT is a general IT-governance framework.
why_others_are_wrong.B: ISO 15489 is a records-management standard.
why_others_are_wrong.D: AACS is a DRM scheme.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps health-information framework to HITRUST.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Selecting Security Controls

questions.question: Match each framework (1-4) to its primary description (A-D).

options.label: A
options.text: International code of practice with security control objectives

options.label: B
options.text: Financial-reporting framework that drives SOX 404 compliance

options.label: C
options.text: IT governance framework managed by ISACA

options.label: D
options.text: U.S. federal security control catalog with control families (required by FISMA)

explanation.why_correct: COBIT → IT governance/ISACA (B); COSO → financial reporting/SOX 404 (A); ISO/IEC 27002 → international control objectives (D); NIST SP 800-53 → U.S. federal control families/FISMA (C).

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests precise mapping of control frameworks to their purposes.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Important Terms

questions.question: Log monitoring and an intrusion detection system are examples of which control type?

explanation.why_correct: Detective controls identify incidents after they happen, e.g., log monitoring and intrusion detection systems.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Preventative controls stop incidents from happening (e.g., firewalls, authentication).
why_others_are_wrong.D: Recovery controls return systems to normal after an incident (e.g., DR plans).
why_others_are_wrong.A: Deterrent controls discourage incidents (e.g., warning banners).

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps log monitoring/IDS to detective controls.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Types within Defense in Depth Strategy

questions.question: Backup recovery and patch management, used to remedy an incident after detection, are examples of which control type?

explanation.why_correct: Corrective controls remedy an incident after detection, e.g., backup recovery and patch management.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Deterrent controls discourage incidents before they occur.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Directive controls mandate behaviors (e.g., policies).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Preventative controls stop incidents from happening in the first place.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps remediation-after-detection to corrective controls.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Control Types within Defense in Depth Strategy

questions.question: In the Deming Cycle (PDCA) applied to security controls, which step assesses whether implemented controls are effective and meet security goals?

explanation.why_correct: In PDCA, "Check" assesses the effectiveness of controls and whether they meet security goals.

why_others_are_wrong.D: "Plan" identifies objectives and determines appropriate controls.
why_others_are_wrong.B: "Do" implements the selected controls.
why_others_are_wrong.C: "Act" addresses gaps in effectiveness, especially after incidents or changes.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the assessment step of PDCA.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > The Deming Cycle (PDCA)

questions.question: Which technology blocks unauthorized data exfiltration by performing egress monitoring and pattern matching against classifications like PII and PHI?

explanation.why_correct: DLP blocks unauthorized data exfiltration (egress monitoring) and uses pattern matching to act on classified data such as PII or PHI.

why_others_are_wrong.B: DRM enforces copyright protection on digital media via encryption.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A TPM secures cryptographic keys/data at rest on a device.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Degaussing is a magnetic data-destruction method.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps exfiltration prevention/egress monitoring to DLP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Data Loss Prevention (DLP)

questions.question: A DLP deployment that scans local file systems and monitors data leaving individual laptops is which type of DLP?

explanation.why_correct: Endpoint DLP scans local file systems and monitors data leaving individual endpoints to detect and block exfiltration.

why_others_are_wrong.C: Network DLP scans outgoing data on the network rather than on the endpoint.
why_others_are_wrong.A: "Cloud DLP gateway" is not the term used; CASB provides cloud DLP functions.
why_others_are_wrong.B: A firewall filters traffic but is not specifically endpoint DLP.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes endpoint DLP from network DLP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Types of DLP

questions.question: For DLP software to reliably detect and act on sensitive data, that data must FIRST be:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypted with a key the DLP cannot access

options.label: B
options.text: Labeled or classified so the DLP policies can recognize it

explanation.why_correct: DLP relies on data being labeled or classified so its policies can detect and act on it; regular updates are also needed for performance.

why_others_are_wrong.A: If DLP cannot inspect the data, it cannot enforce policy on it; this defeats detection.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Deleting data removes the very thing DLP is meant to protect.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Making data public is the opposite of protecting it from exfiltration.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests the classification prerequisite for effective DLP.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Types of DLP

questions.question: A Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) primarily functions as:

options.label: B
options.text: A magnetic device for destroying backup tapes

options.label: C
options.text: A security policy enforcement point (proxy) between users and cloud services

options.label: D
options.text: A hardware root of trust embedded in a CPU

explanation.why_correct: A CASB is a policy enforcement point that acts as a proxy between users and cloud services, applying data security, DLP, threat protection, and URL filtering.

why_others_are_wrong.B: That describes a degausser.
why_others_are_wrong.A: That describes a standard like ISO 15489.
why_others_are_wrong.D: That describes a TPM.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps cloud policy enforcement to CASB.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB)

questions.question: Digital Rights Management (DRM) primarily uses encryption to:

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor outbound network traffic for PII

options.label: C
options.text: Track which employees badge into a facility

options.label: D
options.text: Enforce copyright protection and prevent unauthorized copying/sharing of digital media

explanation.why_correct: DRM uses encryption to enforce copyright protection for digital media and prevent copying, piracy, and unauthorized sharing.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Monitoring outbound traffic for PII is DLP's role.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Media sanitization is a destruction activity, not DRM.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Badge tracking is a physical access control, not DRM.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps copyright/anti-piracy enforcement to DRM.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Data Protection Methods

questions.question: A company is most worried that employees might email spreadsheets full of customer PII to personal accounts. Which protection method MOST directly addresses this exfiltration risk?

options.label: A
options.text: A Trusted Platform Module on each laptop

options.label: B
options.text: Digital Rights Management (DRM) for media files

options.label: C
options.text: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) with egress monitoring

explanation.why_correct: DLP with egress monitoring detects and blocks unauthorized transfer of classified data such as PII leaving the organization.

why_others_are_wrong.B: DRM protects copyrighted media from copying, not general PII exfiltration via email.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Degaussing destroys data on tapes; it does not stop email exfiltration.
why_others_are_wrong.A: A TPM protects keys/data at rest on a device, not data being emailed out.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests selecting DLP for an exfiltration scenario.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Data Protection Methods

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are data protection methods described in the guide? (Select TWO.)

explanation.why_correct: DLP and CASB are data protection methods; the others are an asset tier and a classification level.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Tier 0 (Essential) is an asset classification tier, not a protection method.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Unclassified is a data classification level, not a protection method.

questions.exam_reasoning: Separates protection methods from classification constructs.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Important Terms

questions.question: Data remanence refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: Leftover data that remains after an attempt to delete or remove it

options.label: B
options.text: Data currently being processed in memory

options.label: C
options.text: A type of cloud access broker

options.label: D
options.text: Data that has been classified as Top Secret

explanation.why_correct: Data remanence is leftover data that remains after deletion attempts; simple deletion often just moves data (e.g., to a recycle bin) rather than destroying it.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Classification level is unrelated to remanence.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Data in memory is data in use, not remanence.
why_others_are_wrong.C: A CASB is a cloud security proxy, not remanence.

questions.exam_reasoning: Recall of the data-remanence definition.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Managing Data Remanence

questions.question: Which destruction technique involves REPEATED clearing (overwriting) to ensure data is completely unrecoverable, often used in highly sensitive government or medical environments?

explanation.why_correct: Purging is repeated clearing to ensure data is completely unrecoverable, common in highly sensitive environments.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Erasing only deletes from the file system and is not effective against remnants.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Clearing overwrites once; purging repeats clearing for stronger assurance.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Labeling is a handling identification activity, not destruction.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes purging (repeated clearing) from erasing and clearing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Data Destruction Techniques

questions.question: An administrator "deletes" sensitive files and empties the recycle bin before donating the hard drive. Why is this insufficient to prevent data disclosure?

options.label: A
options.text: Erasing physically shreds the platters, which is unnecessary

options.label: B
options.text: Erasing removes file-system references but leaves recoverable data remnants on the disk

options.label: D
options.text: Erasing encrypts the data so strongly it cannot be read

explanation.why_correct: Erasing deletes the file-system reference but does not remove the data from the disk, leaving recoverable remnants; clearing/purging/sanitization is required.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Erasing does not physically destroy platters; that would be a separate method.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Erasing does not encrypt data.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Erasing does not perform degaussing.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests why simple deletion fails to prevent data remanence.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Data Destruction Techniques

questions.question: Which sanitization method uses strong magnetic fields to scramble data and is effective for magnetic media such as backup tapes?

explanation.why_correct: Degaussing uses strong magnetic fields to scramble data on magnetic media (e.g., backup tapes), making it unrecoverable.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Zeroing overwrites the medium with zeros and is not magnetic destruction.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Tokenization substitutes data with non-sensitive tokens (a protection method).
why_others_are_wrong.C: Pseudonymization replaces data with aliases (a declassification technique).

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps magnetic-media destruction to degaussing.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Data Sanitization Methods

questions.question: A best practice is to choose the sanitization method based on the storage medium. Which pairing follows this guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Zeroing for paper documents; marking for SSDs

options.label: B
options.text: Degaussing for solid-state drives; tokenizing for tapes

options.label: C
options.text: Degaussing for magnetic tapes; overwriting for hard drives

options.label: D
options.text: Pseudonymization for hard drives; labeling for tapes

explanation.why_correct: The guide recommends matching method to medium—e.g., degaussing for tapes and overwriting for hard drives.

why_others_are_wrong.B: Degaussing is for magnetic media (not SSDs), and tokenization is a protection method, not sanitization for tapes.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Pseudonymization and labeling are not media-sanitization methods.
why_others_are_wrong.A: Zeroing applies to digital media, not paper; marking is handling, not SSD sanitization.

questions.exam_reasoning: Tests matching sanitization methods to the appropriate media.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Best Practices for Data Remnant Management

questions.question: Which declassification technique substitutes sensitive data with non-sensitive tokens that have no intrinsic value, requiring a separate mapping to recover the original data?

explanation.why_correct: Tokenization substitutes sensitive data with meaningless tokens; the tokens must be mapped back to the original for internal use but appear valueless to unauthorized users.

why_others_are_wrong.A: Pseudonymization replaces data with aliases that can still be linked back through separate records, but is not specifically the non-intrinsic-value token mechanism described.
why_others_are_wrong.D: Obfuscation conceals/masks data (e.g., a black box over text).
why_others_are_wrong.B: De-identification removes personal identifiers to anonymize data.

questions.exam_reasoning: Distinguishes tokenization from other declassification techniques.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Declassification Techniques

questions.question: Removing personal identifiers (such as account numbers) from medical records so the data can no longer be linked to a specific person is called:

explanation.why_correct: De-identification removes personal identifiers to prevent linking data to a specific subject, anonymizing it.

why_others_are_wrong.D: Tokenization substitutes data with mapped tokens, not identifier removal for anonymization.
why_others_are_wrong.C: Degaussing is magnetic media destruction.
why_others_are_wrong.B: Scoping selects which controls apply to a system.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps identifier removal/anonymization to de-identification.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Declassification Techniques

questions.question: Which NIST Special Publication provides guidelines for media sanitization?

explanation.why_correct: NIST SP 800-88 provides guidelines for media sanitization.

why_others_are_wrong.B: NIST SP 800-60 covers data types and classification.
why_others_are_wrong.A: NIST SP 800-37 is the Risk Management Framework.
why_others_are_wrong.C: NIST SP 800-53 is the security/privacy control catalog.

questions.exam_reasoning: Maps media-sanitization guidance to NIST SP 800-88.

source_reference.syllabus_section: Domain 2 > Data Security Controls > Regulations and Guidelines
